text:
Lukas Dostal faced 11 shots and three of them went in. By the first intermission Calgary led 3-1, and the Flames looked like the team that had beaten Anaheim 4-2 back on Oct. 13. Ville Husso took over in the Ducks' net, stopped all 10 shots he saw, and the rest of the night belonged to Anaheim.

The first period was a mess for Anaheim. William Stromgren scored on a backhand at 2:23, Jeff Malott answered at 2:50, and then Joel Hanley's point shot at 16:29 and Joel Farabee's power-play snap shot at 19:02 (an 8% chance) put the Flames up two. Zayne Parekh, the ninth overall pick in 2024, set up two of the three.

Then the ice tilted. Calgary had won the first period on expected goals (the quality of the chances each side created) 1.40 to 1.06. Anaheim won the second 1.28 to 0.58 and the third 1.56 to 0.42. Tristan Luneau cut it to 3-2 at 12:02 of the second, and Leo Carlsson tied it on the power play 55 seconds into the third, a goal that lifted the Ducks' win chance from 28% to 52%.

The winner came from nowhere. With 1:34 left, Cutter Gauthier let a slap shot go that our numbers gave a 2% chance of scoring, and it beat Dustin Wolf. That one swing took Anaheim from 48% to 89% and was worth 0.41 wins, the most of anyone on the night. Nikita Nesterenko added another at 19:46. Beckett Sennecke and Mikael Granlund assisted on both of the third-period goals that decided it.

This was not a smash-and-grab. The Ducks out-attempted Calgary 65 to 47 and deserved to win 60% of the time (the share of replays of every shot that a team wins). That is four straight wins, and the season series with the Flames now leans their way. The one thing you'd circle if you were Anaheim is Dostal: 1.6 goals worse than his shots deserved, in a period the team was already losing.
headline: Ducks climb out of a 3-1 hole in Calgary
